anchor: Do ye hear the children weeping
title: Occasion: the child labour reports
short: Written in response to the Children's Employment Commission reports (1842-43), and first printed in Blackwood's, August 1843.
body: The Royal Commission on Children's Employment published a report on mines in 1842, with evidence of very young children working underground, and a second report on trades and manufactures in 1843. Barrett's friend the poet R. H. Horne was one of the sub-commissioners, and the evidence he gathered is said to have prompted her poem. The poem appeared in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine in August 1843 and was reprinted, revised, in Poems (1844). It became one of the best-known texts of the factory reform movement associated with Lord Ashley (later Shaftesbury).

title: The epigraph from Medea
greek: φεῦ φεῦ, τί προσδέρκεσθέ μ’ ὄμμασιν, τέκνα;
short: Medea's words to her children before she kills them: 'Alas, alas, why do you look at me with your eyes, children?'
body: The epigraph, added in 1844, quotes Euripides' Medea (l. 1040) in transliterated Greek. Medea, about to murder her sons to punish Jason, falters at their gaze. Barrett's implication is fierce: England is a mother destroying its own children, and the children's gaze, like that of Medea's sons, accuses. The theme of the children looking up 'with their pale and sunken faces' (st. 3, 13) answers the epigraph. The use of Greek also announces the learned, prophetic authority of a woman poet addressing public questions.

title: 'O my brothers': address and metre
short: The poem addresses the nation (and its men, who held political power) as 'brothers', in long, loosely trochaic lines.
body: The repeated apostrophe 'O my brothers' casts the speaker as a prophet or preacher addressing the men who make laws and own mills. The long lines are predominantly trochaic (stress-unstress: 'DO ye HEAR the CHILdren WEEPing'), alternating with shorter lines, with a heavy, chant-like rhythm. The stanzas are mostly of twelve lines (the fourth runs to sixteen) rhyming in alternate lines. Barrett used many inexact rhymes ('children / bewildering', 'stilled in / children'), which drew criticism as careless; she treated such rhyme as a legitimate experiment.

anchor: In the country of the free
title: 'the country of the free'; 'our happy Fatherland'
short: Bitter irony: England, proud of abolishing slavery, still works its own children like slaves.
body: The British Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 was a source of national pride, and anti-slavery language was often turned against industrial conditions at home, with factory children called 'white slaves'. Barrett herself came from a family whose wealth derived from Jamaican plantations. 'The country of the free' and 'our happy Fatherland' are ironic, and stanza 12 makes the comparison explicit: the children 'Are slaves, without the liberty in Christdom'. The opening contrast with lambs, birds, fawns and flowers places the children outside the natural order of youth.

title: the old faces of children
short: The children's faces bear 'the man's hoary anguish', as if grief belonging to old age were pressed onto infancy.
body: 'Hoary' (grey-haired, aged) anguish 'draws and presses / Down the cheeks of infancy'. The paradox of children who are old before their time runs through the poem: they are 'weary' after 'few paces', and their 'grave-rest is very far to seek'. The line returns almost unchanged in the last stanza ('They look up with their pale and sunken faces'), where 'looks are sad' becomes 'look is dread', a turn from pity to accusation. The image answers the epigraph's children whose gaze Medea cannot bear.

title: Little Alice
short: The children envy dead Alice, whose grave is 'shapen / Like a snowball' in the frost, because she can rest.
body: Stanza 4 is spoken by the children, who report that 'It is good when it happens ... / That we die before our time.' Alice's grave is a small mound in the 'rime' (hoarfrost). There 'Was no room for any work in the close clay', a grim joke: the grave is the one place without labour. No one will wake her with 'Get up, little Alice! it is day', recalling the early-morning summons to work. Child mortality in the mines and mills was a central concern of the reports.

title: kirk-chime
short: 'Kirk' is Scots and northern English for church: Alice lies in her shroud near the church bells.
body: The northern word 'kirk' fits the industrial north and Scotland, where many mills and mines were. Alice's moments, 'lulled and stilled in / The shroud by the kirk-chime', are 'merry' because still. This is one of the poem's controversial rhymes ('stilled in' / 'children'), which links the dead girl to the living. The sound of church bells, a promise of rest, is set against the noise of the iron wheels later.

anchor: With a cerement from the grave
title: cerement
short: A 'cerement' is a waxed cloth wrapping a corpse; the children bind their hearts in grave-clothes to keep them from breaking.
body: From Latin cera, wax, the cerement or cerecloth was used to wrap the dead (Hamlet speaks of his father's 'cerements', 1.4.48). The image is of children who, seeking 'Death in life', numb their feelings in advance. When the speaker urges them to go out into the meadows and pick cowslips, they answer that meadow flowers are nothing to them, 'Like our weeds anear the mine'; they want only to be left 'in the dark of the coal-shadows'.

title: the mines and factories
short: The children describe two forms of labour: dragging coal in mines and tending the machines in factories.
body: The 1842 report described children, some as young as five or six, working as 'trappers' (opening ventilation doors) and 'hurriers' (dragging coal tubs, sometimes harnessed by chains) in narrow seams, 'Our knees tremble sorely in the stooping'. The Mines Act of 1842 banned underground work for women and for boys under ten. The 'wheels of iron / In the factories, round and round' refer to the textile mills, where long hours were regulated by the Factory Act of 1833, with further reform in 1844 and the Ten Hours Act of 1847.

title: the turning wheels
short: Everything turns: wheels, hearts, heads, walls, sky, light, flies, 'and we with all', mimicking the giddiness of machine labour.
body: Stanza 7 is the poem's most striking rendering of industrial experience. The repetition of 'turn' (seven times) and the inverted syntax ('Turns the sky ... / Turns the long light ... / Turn the black flies') reproduce the dizziness of children who stand for hours beside revolving machinery. The 'wind' of the wheels blows in their faces. The children's only prayer is to the wheels: 'Stop! be silent for to-day!' In stanza 8 the speaker takes up their cry ('Ay, be silent!'), insisting that the 'cold metallic motion / Is not all the life God fashions or reveals'.

title: souls called 'sunward' but spinning in the dark
short: God calls the children's souls toward the light, but they 'Spin on blindly in the dark' like the machines.
body: The souls are imagined as being turned by the wheels, 'Grinding life down from its mark' (from its aim or its natural measure). 'Sunward' recalls the earlier contrast with flowers that 'blow toward the west' and anticipates stanza 12: 'They have never seen the sunshine, nor the glory / Which is brighter than the sun' (God's glory, Revelation 21:23, 'the glory of God did lighten it'). Spinning is both factory work and blind, purposeless motion.

title: 'Our Father'
short: The children know only the first two words of the Lord's Prayer, which they say like a charm at night.
body: The 1842-43 reports recorded the shocking ignorance of many working children, who could not name Christ or say a prayer; the children here know 'no other words except "Our Father"' (Matthew 6:9). They hope God might 'pluck them' out of the angels' song and hold them in his right hand. The pathos lies in the gap between the universal fatherhood of God invoked in the prayer and the absence of any father, earthly or heavenly, who seems to hear.

anchor: He is speechless as a stone
title: 'He is speechless as a stone'
short: The children conclude that God is dumb, and that the master who commands them is said to be 'of His image'.
body: The children's despair is theological: 'they tell us, of His image is the master / Who commands us to work on' (man made in God's image, Genesis 1:27). If the master is God's image, God must be like the master. 'Go to!' is an archaic exclamation of impatience or disbelief (as in Genesis 11:3-4). The speaker then generalises: 'For God's possible is taught by His world's loving', that is, people learn what God might be from the love they meet in the world. The stanza was bold for 1843, charging social injustice with producing atheism.

title: Christdom; martyrs without the palm
short: The children suffer like slaves and martyrs without the compensations of Christian freedom or the martyr's palm.
body: 'Christdom', a coinage or rare variant for Christendom, means the realm of Christ, where (St Paul says) servants are 'the Lord's freeman' (1 Corinthians 7:22). The 'palm' is the symbol of the martyr's victory (Revelation 7:9, the multitude 'with palms in their hands'). The children have the pain of martyrdom ('the pang') without its reward, the grief of age without its wisdom, and they 'Are orphans of the earthly love and heavenly'. The stanza ends with the speaker's exhausted 'Let them weep! let them weep!'

title: 'their angels in high places'
short: Christ warned that children's angels always behold the face of God: the angels are witnesses against their oppressors.
body: Matthew 18:10: 'Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones; for I say unto you, That in heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father.' The children's look reminds the 'brothers' of these angels 'With eyes turned on Deity'. The cry 'How long ... how long, O cruel nation' echoes the martyrs under the altar in Revelation 6:10 ('How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood'), and the Psalms (13:1).

anchor: Stifle down with a mailed heel
title: the mailed heel, the mart, the gold-heaper
short: The nation stands on a child's heart to move the world, crushing it under an armoured heel on its way to a throne in the market.
body: The image of standing on something 'to move the world' recalls Archimedes' boast that with a place to stand he could move the earth; here the fulcrum of national power is a child's heart. The 'mailed heel' is armoured like a knight's, and the 'throne amid the mart' (market) combines imperial pride with commerce. The 'gold-heaper' is the capitalist whose 'purple' (the royal colour) is stained by the children's 'blood splash[ing] upward'. The final couplet claims that 'the child's sob in the silence curses deeper / Than the strong man in his wrath', a prophetic threat.

title: Barrett's rhymes
short: 'Children' is rhymed with 'bewildering' and 'stilled in': imperfect rhymes that troubled contemporary readers.
body: Barrett's experimental rhymes (also 'Heaven / unbelieving' in st. 11 and 'unretrievingly / heavenly' in st. 12) drew complaints of carelessness from reviewers of the 1844 Poems. Such rhymes belong to her deliberate experiments with rhyme in these years, though reviewers took them for lapses. In this poem the half-rhymes on 'children' are effective: the word that should be the centre of the stanza never finds a true partner, as the children find no place. 'Without' here means outside.
